content.heading: 2.8 Subspaces of ℝn
content.paragraph: This section focuses on important sets of vectors in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ called subspaces. Often subspaces arise in connection with some matrix $A$, and they provide useful information about the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$. The concepts and terminology in this section will be used repeatedly throughout the rest of the book.1

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is any set $H$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ that has three properties:

list.item: The zero vector is in H.﻿
For each u and v in H, the sum u+v is in H.﻿
For each u in H and each scalar c, the vector cu is in H.﻿

content.paragraph: In words, a subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. As you will see in the next few examples, most sets of vectors discussed in Chapter 1 are subspaces. For instance, a plane through the origin is the standard way to visualize the subspace in Example 1. See Figure 1.

image.alt: A graph shows a tilted parallelogram plane resting on a three-dimensional axis.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ are in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ and $H = \text{Span}\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$, then $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. To verify this statement, note that the zero vector is in $H$ (because $0\textbf{v}_{1} + 0\textbf{v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2})$. Also, for any scalar $c$, the vector $c\textbf{u}$ is in $H$, because $c\textbf{u} = c(s_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + s_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}) = (cs_{1})\textbf{v}_{1} + (cs_{2})\textbf{v}_{2}$.﻿

content.paragraph: If $\textbf{v}_{1}$ is not zero and if $\textbf{v}_{2}$ is a multiple of $\textbf{v}_{1}$, then $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ simply span a line through the origin. So a line through the origin is another example of a subspace.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: For $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\text{,}$ the set of all linear combinations of $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. The verification of this statement is similar to the argument given in Example 1. We shall now refer to $\text{Span}\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ as the subspace spanned (or generated) by $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$.﻿

content.paragraph: Note that $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is a subspace of itself because it has the three properties required for a subspace. Another special subspace is the set consisting of only the zero vector in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. This set, called the zero subspace, also satisfies the conditions for a subspace.
content.heading: Column Space and Null Space of a Matrix
content.paragraph: Subspaces of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ usually occur in applications and theory in one of two ways. In both cases, the subspace can be related to a matrix.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The column space of a matrix $A$ is the set $\text{Col }A$ of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$.﻿

content.paragraph: The solution of Example 4 shows that when a system of linear equations is written in the form $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$, the column space of $A$ is the set of all $\textbf{b}$ for which the system has a solution.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The null space of a matrix $A$ is the set $\text{Nul }A$ of all solutions of the homogeneous equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$.﻿

content.paragraph: When $A$ has $n$ columns, the solutions of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ belong to $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, and the null space of $A$ is a subset of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. In fact, $\text{Nul }A$ has the properties of a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.﻿

note.title: Theorem 12
note.heading: Theorem 12
note.paragraph: The null space of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. Equivalently, the set of all solutions of a system $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ of $m$ homogeneous linear equations in $n$ unknowns is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: The zero vector is in $\text{Nul }A$ (because $A\textbf{0} = \textbf{0}$). To show that $\text{Nul }A$ satisfies the other two properties required for a subspace, take any $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ in $\text{Nul }A$ That is, suppose $A\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$ and $A\textbf{v} = \textbf{0}$. Then, by a property of matrix multiplication,

Thus $\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$ satisfies $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$, and so $\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$ is in $\text{Nul }A$. Also, for any scalar $c,A(c\textbf{u}) =$ $c\left( A\textbf{u} \right) = c\left( \textbf{0} \right) = \textbf{0}$, which shows that $c\textbf{u}$ is in $\text{Nul }A$.﻿

To test whether a given vector $\textbf{v}$ is in $\text{Nul }A$, just compute $A\textbf{v}$ to see whether $A\textbf{v}$ is the zero vector. Because $\text{Nul }A$ is described by a condition that must be checked for each vector, we say that the null space is defined implicitly. In contrast, the column space is defined explicitly, because vectors in $\text{Col }A$ can be constructed (by linear combinations) from the columns of $A$. To create an explicit description of $\text{Nul }A$, solve the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ and write the solution in parametric vector form. (See Example 6.)2
content.heading: Basis for a Subspace
content.paragraph: Because a subspace typically contains an infinite number of vectors, some problems involving a subspace are handled best by working with a small finite set of vectors that span the subspace. The smaller the set, the better. It can be shown that the smallest possible spanning set must be linearly independent.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A basic for a subspace $H$ of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is a linearly independent set in $H$ that spans $H$.﻿

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: The columns of an invertible $n \times n$ matrix form a basis for all of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ because they are linearly independent and span $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, by the Invertible Matrix Theorem. One such matrix is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Its columns are denoted by $\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{e}_{n}$:
The set $\{\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{e}_{n}\}$ is called the standard basis for $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. See Figure 3.

image.alt: A figure shows three vectors along the three-dimensional axis.

content.paragraph: The next example shows that the standard procedure for writing the solution set of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ in parametric vector form actually identifies a basis for $\text{Nul }A$ This fact will be used throughout Chapter 5.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the null space of the matrix
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, write the solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ in parametric vector form:
The general solution is $x_{1} = 2x_{2} + x_{4} - 3x_{5}\text{,}$ $x_{3} = - 2x_{4} + 2x_{5}\text{,}$ with $x_{2}\text{,}$ $x_{4}\text{,}$ and $x_{5}$ free.

Equation (1) shows that $\text{Nul }A$ coincides with the set of all linear combinations of $\textbf{u}\text{,}$ $\textbf{v},$ and $\textbf{w}\text{.}$ That is, $\{\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\textbf{w}\}$ generates $\text{Nul }A$. In fact, this construction of $\textbf{u}\text{,}$ $\textbf{v}\text{,}$ and $\textbf{w}$ automatically makes them linearly independent, because equation (1) shows that $\textbf{0} = x_{2}\textbf{u} + x_{4}\textbf{v} + x_{5}\textbf{w}$ only if the weights $x_{2}\text{,}$ $x_{4}\text{,}$ and $x_{5}$ are all zero. (Examine entries $2$, $4$, and $5$ in the vector $x_{2}\textbf{u} + x_{4}\textbf{v} + x_{5}\textbf{w}$.) So $\{\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\textbf{w}\}$ is a basis for $\text{Nul }A$.﻿

content.paragraph: Finding a basis for the column space of a matrix is actually less work than finding a basis for the null space. However, the method requires some explanation. Let’s begin with a simple case.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the column space of the matrix
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Denote the columns of $B$ by $\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{5}$ and note that $\textbf{b}_{3} = - 3\textbf{b}_{1} + 2\textbf{b}_{2}$ and $\textbf{b}_{4} = 5\textbf{b}_{1} - \textbf{b}_{2}$. The fact that $\textbf{b}_{3}$ and $\textbf{b}_{4}$ are combinations of the pivot columns means that any combination of $\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{5}$ is actually just a combination of $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{5}$. Indeed, if $\textbf{v}$ is any vector in $\text{Col }B$, say,
then, substituting for $\textbf{b}_{3}$ and $\textbf{b}_{4}$, we can write $\textbf{v}$ in the form

which is a linear combination of $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{5}$ So $\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1} \right.$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, $\left. \textbf{b}_{5} \right\}$ spans $\text{Col }B$ Also, $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{5}$ are linearly independent, because they are columns from an identity matrix. So the pivot columns of $B$ form a basis for $\text{Col }B$.﻿

content.paragraph: The matrix $B$ in Example 7 is in reduced echelon form. To handle a general matrix $A\text{,}$ recall that linear dependence relations among the columns of $A$ can be expressed in the form $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ for some $\textbf{x}$. (If some columns are not involved in a particular dependence relation, then the corresponding entries in $\textbf{x}$ are zero.) When $A$ is row reduced to echelon form $B$, the columns are drastically changed, but the equations $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ and $B\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ have the same set of solutions. That is, the columns of $A$ have exactly the same linear dependence relationships as the columns of $B$.﻿

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: From Example 7, the pivot columns of $A$ are columns $1$, $2$, and $5$. Also, $\textbf{b}_{3} = - 3\textbf{b}_{1} + 2\textbf{b}_{2}$ and $\textbf{b}_{4} = 5\textbf{b}_{1} - \textbf{b}_{2}$. Since row operations do not affect linear dependence relations among the columns of the matrix, we should have

Check that this is true! By the argument in Example 7, $\textbf{a}_{3}$ and $\textbf{a}_{4}$ are not needed to generate the column space of $A$. Also, $\left\{ \textbf{a}_{1},\,\textbf{a}_{2},\,\textbf{a}_{5} \right\}$ must be linearly independent, because any dependence relation among $\textbf{a}_{1}\text{,}$ $\textbf{a}_{2}\text{,}$ and $\textbf{a}_{5}$ would imply the same dependence relation among $\textbf{b}_{1}\text{,}$ $\textbf{b}_{2}\text{,}$ and $\textbf{b}_{5}$. Since $\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1},\,\textbf{b}_{2},\,\textbf{b}_{5} \right\}$ is linearly independent, $\left\{ \textbf{a}_{1},\,\textbf{a}_{2},\,\textbf{a}_{5} \right\}$ is also linearly independent and hence is a basis for $\text{Col }A$.﻿

content.paragraph: The argument in Example8 can be adapted to prove the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 13
note.heading: Theorem 13
note.paragraph: The pivot columns of a matrix $A$ form a basis for the column space of $A$.﻿

content.paragraph: Warning: Be careful to use pivot columns of$A$itself for the basis of $\text{Col }A$. The columns of an echelon form $B$ are often not in the column space of $A$. (For instance, in Examples 7 and 8, the columns of $B$ all have zeros in their last entries and cannot generate the columns of $A$.)

statement.paragraph: (T/F) A subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is any set $H$ such that (i) the zero vector is in $H$, (ii) $\textbf{u}$, $\textbf{v}$, and $\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$ are in $H$, and (iii) $c$ is a scalar and $c\textbf{u}$ is in $H$.﻿
(T/F) A subset $H$ of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is a subspace if the zero vector is in $H$.﻿

(T/F) If $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ are in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, then Span $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ is the same as the column space of the matrix $\lbrack\textbf{v}_{1}\ldots\textbf{v}_{p}\rbrack$.﻿
(T/F) Given vectors $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, the set of all linear combinations of these vectors is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.﻿
(T/F) The set of all solutions of a system of $m$ homogeneous equations in $n$ unknowns is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$.﻿
(T/F) The null space of an $m \times n$ matrix is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.﻿
(T/F) The columns of an invertible $n \times n$ matrix form a basis for $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.﻿
(T/F) The column space of a matrix $A$ is the set of solutions of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$.﻿
